newsitem.title: UK: Metal premiums stable in Europe, but physicals slo.
newsitem.headline: Metal premiums stable in Europe, but physicals slo.

text.p: European base metal physical business has not been particularly active this week, although premiums have largely held steady across the board.
Traders said consumers were maintaining their usual policy of running hand-to-mouth strategies - hence the low level of spot trading in most physical metals.
"People tend to hold off when it (the market) is up - and come in when it is down," one copper trader said.
There has been little significant movement in copper premiums or discounts for standard cathode, although this may change in the near-term, some said.
Firstly, the backwardation on the London Metal Exchange is contracting, which will hopefully encourage more spot interest.
Also, there are signs that scrap might be tightening up again, as happened in the last quarter of 1996.
"Demand for scrap is quite good at the moment, and there is not that much of it around," one U.K. scrap trader said.
This may see the scrap discount, currently around 75 stg, contract, as well as secondary refiners having to use primary metal for feed.
In aluminium, the high spot premiums in the U.S. Midwest of some seven cents/lb are likely to continue to suck metal from Europe acrss the Atlantic.
European premiums are presently holding steady, but are seen moving higher if this trend in metal movements is maintained.
Traders said business has been at the higher end of quotes, and there has been some talk of Western ingots trading as high as $55, although this may just be an isolated transaction.
Whether this firmness can continue through the second quarter is debatable, however. Producer to fabricator orders look good, but further downstream activity may not be so keen, some said.
In tin, there has been little movement in premiums and activity, although a perk-up on the LME and a contraction in the contango may change this pattern.
Cash/threes has narrowed to near parity from $40 two days ago, reflecting May/threes tightness and borrowing of speculative short positions.
"The premiums will head down a little becuase of the tightness," one tin specialist said.
